# Good Night, and Good Luck: AI, fear and what the job data says

Hi all,

A couple of weeks ago, an email reminded me of Good Night, and Good Luck (2005), the film by George Clooney. It tells the story of Edward R. Murrow, the CBS journalist who stood up to Senator Joseph McCarthy in 1954. McCarthy accused people of being disloyal to their country, and claimed he had a secret list of 205 names working in the State Department ( Wikipedia ). Being accused was enough to lose your job.

McCarthy did not need proof. He only needed people to be scared. Fear got attention, and attention gave him power.

That story made me think about my X.com feed. Every day I read that AI will replace software engineers in 6 months. Some of those posts come from people who are paid by engagement (blue checks). Others come from companies whose valuation grows when AI looks more powerful (and more dangerous).

So I wanted to check the data myself. Is AI really destroying software jobs? Or is something else going on?

At the end I will give my opinion (my own, not my employer’s). All sources are linked.

## 1. What the AI reports say

There are two big yearly reports about AI. Let’s see what they say about 2025 and 2026.

### Stanford AI Index 2026

The AI Index 2026 was published in April 2026. These are the points I found more relevant:

- global corporate investment in AI was $581.7 billion in 2025, up 130%. The US invested $285.9B, China $12.4B

- AI agents went from 20% to 77.3% on Terminal Bench (real tasks in a terminal) in one year. But they still fail at multistep planning, financial analysis and even telling the time.

- employment among software developers aged 22-25 has fallen nearly 20% since 2024, even as older colleagues’ headcount grows. Their own words: “The disruption is targeted and just beginning.”

- only 33% of Americans expect AI to improve their jobs

### State of AI Report 2026

The State of AI Report was published in October 2026:

- OpenAI and Anthropic together reached $105B in annualized revenue by late summer 2026 (from $30B at the start of the year)

- The four big US cloud companies plan around $733B of capex in 2026.

- Benchmarks are getting saturated “within months”.

- The harness matters a lot. In one study, only changing “the tools, context, and feedback” given to a model (GLM-5.1) moved it from 52.5% to 65.5% on SWE-bench Verified tasks. Same model, same weights.

- The cost to reach a fixed benchmark score falls around 13x per year. Intelligence is getting very cheap.

AI is improving fast and money is flowing like never before. But does this show in the job market?

## 2. Software jobs and what the data says

Indeed Hiring Lab publishes daily job postings data by country and by sector. It is an index: 100 means the same number of job postings as on 1 February 2020 (just before the pandemic). I used the data until 9 October 2026.

I compared the “Software Development” sector with all job postings, and I marked the main AI releases.

### The US

Look at the date of the peak: 28 February 2022 . ChatGPT was released on 30 November 2022, nine months later.

When ChatGPT was released, software job postings in the US had already dropped 39% from the peak. More than half (53%) of the total fall happened before ChatGPT existed.

So what happened in early 2022? Look at the bottom chart. The US Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time on 16 March 2022, two weeks after the peak. Rates went from 0.08% to 5.33% in about a year and a half ( Federal Reserve ). In Europe, the ECB moved its deposit rate from -0.50% to 4.00% ( ECB ).

This matters a lot for software. A software project costs money today and makes money in the future. When money is free, companies hire a lot of engineers to build things that maybe will pay back in 5 years. When money costs 5%, they stop.

There are two more things to keep in mind:

- The pandemic bubble. Software postings reached 2.3x the pre pandemic level. A lot of the “collapse” is that bubble deflating. Companies overhired in 2021 and corrected in 2022 and 2023. We all know cases.

- From 2022, US companies could not deduct software developer salaries immediately as R&D, they had to spread the deduction over 5 years. This was fixed in July 2025 ( Eide Bailly ). However, I did not find a serious study measuring its effect on hiring.

### jobs vs LLM model released

This is the index of software postings in the US on the day of each big release:

Since May 2025, software postings in the US are going up (+28%), while all job postings are flat. This is exactly the period of the best coding models and coding agents ever 🤔

Indeed found the same in their own analysis from July 2026 : software postings grew almost 15% since Claude Code launched, while all postings fell 7%. They are still about 27.5% below the prepandemic level, so it is a recovery from a low point, not a boom.

It is true that job postings are not jobs . Postings measure how many new people companies want to hire. They don’t tell you how many people work in software. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics counts people working in “computer systems design and related services”. That number peaked in March 2023 (2.48 million), after ChatGPT, and it is down 5% since then (2.36 million in September 2026). It is still higher than before the pandemic ( BLS ). So postings fell around 70% from the peak, but the number of people working fell 5%. Companies stopped hiring much more than they fired.

Also, one job posting is not one hire. It can go both ways:

- A company can have headcount for many engineers, publish a single posting (“Senior Backend Engineer”), and keep hiring from it until all the positions are filled.

- Or the opposite: companies publish postings and never hire anyone. These are called “ghost jobs”. Sometimes the reason is just to look like the company is growing. Greenhouse, a recruiting software company, estimated that between 18% and 22% of the postings on its platform were ghost jobs ( Fox News ).

That is why I use postings to see the trend (when companies wanted to hire more or less), and the official employment data to see how many people really work in software.

### Other countries

In all six countries, software postings peaked before ChatGPT.

Germany and France are different. Most of their fall came after ChatGPT, and they are still falling. Is that AI? I am not sure. All job postings are falling there too (France is at 89, below prepandemic), so it looks more like weak economies. Indeed also notes that the software share of job postings is growing in most big economies “outside Germany and France”. In Germany, software development is today the sector with the lowest index of all.

### Is it only software?

No. In the US, the 5 sectors with the lowest index today are Data & Analytics, Media & Communications, IT Infrastructure, Marketing and IT Systems. Mostly white collar jobs that are exposed to AI. So I don’t think AI has zero effect. But the timing tells us the big crash was caused by economics, not by ChatGPT.

## 3. Juniors vs seniors

There is one place where the data really shows an AI effect on young people .

Erik Brynjolfsson and his team at Stanford use payroll data from ADP (millions of US workers). Their paper Canaries in the Coal Mine , updated in August 2026, finds:

- No economy wide job loss.

- But workers aged 22–25 in AI-exposed jobs are 19% below where they would be if they had grown like less exposed jobs.

- Experienced workers don’t show this gap.

- The effect comes from less hiring of young people, not from more firing.

What about interest rates? They checked it in a separate note (February 2026). AI exposed jobs are, on average, less sensitive to interest rates, so rates don’t explain this specific gap well. But they also say that the fall for young software developers “is a consequence of various factors”, and that the AI part only becomes clear in 2024.

The Indeed recovery confirms the same pattern from the other side: 71% of the growth in software postings (May 2025 to May 2026) came from senior roles, and 37% from job titles that include “AI”.

So in summary:

> Economics explains the crash. AI explains the shape of the recovery: fewer juniors, more seniors.

And there is one more number I find important. Fewer people are studying computer science. In the US, undergraduate enrollment in computer and information science at 4 year colleges fell 8.1% in fall 2025, while total enrollment grew ( National Student Clearinghouse ).

## 4. Who profits from fear

### Social media

X.com changed its creator program some time ago. Payouts now depend on how much Premium (blue check) users engage with your posts ( MediaPost ). The post does not need to be true. It needs replies, quotes and shares. And nothing gets more replies than “you will lose your job”.

This is a perverse incentive.

### AI companies

Some quotes from the people who sell AI:

- Jensen Huang (NVIDIA), February 2024: “It is our job to create computing technology such that nobody has to program” ( Computing ).

- Dario Amodei (Anthropic), May 2025: AI could eliminate half of all entry-level white-collar jobs and push unemployment to 10–20% in 1 to 5 years ( Axios ).

And the valuations:

- Anthropic raised $65B at a $965B valuation in May 2026, from $380B in February ( Bloomberg Law ), more than OpenAI.

- NVIDIA is “marching toward a $6T market cap” ( State of AI ).

And it works. Pew Research asked the same question to AI experts and to normal people: will AI have a positive impact on how people do their jobs in the next 20 years? 73% of the experts said yes. Only 23% of the US public said yes ( Pew Research, 2025 ). A 50 point gap between the people who build the technology and the people who read the headlines…

Now, I don’t think all these warnings are lies. Amodei says he talks about it so governments can prepare, and maybe he really believes it. But the incentives point in the same direction: the scarier the AI, the more valuable the company that owns it. When a claim is also a sales pitch, we should check the data.

Fear also moves markets. In February 2026, after Anthropic released plugins for Claude Cowork, around $285B was wiped from software stocks in two weeks. People called it the “SaaSpocalypse”. Then there was a sharp rebound later in the year ( State of AI ).

### What Anthropic says vs. what Anthropic does

In January 2026, at Davos, Dario Amodei said that AI models could do “most, maybe all” of what software engineers do in 6 to 12 months. He also said: “I have engineers within Anthropic who say I don’t write any code anymore. I just let the model write the code, I edit it.” ( Entrepreneur )

Nine months later, did the job disappear? Let’s look at what Anthropic does, not what it says. I counted the open roles on Anthropic’s own job board, month by month, using old snapshots from the Internet Archive:

- In February 2026, just after Davos, Anthropic had 44 open roles with “Software Engineer” in the title. On 21 October 2026 it has 97 . More than double.

- In May 2024 it had 17.

- In total, Anthropic has 674 open roles today, from 102 in May 2024 ( Anthropic job board , data ).

Of course, open roles are not hires, and Anthropic is growing very fast (its revenue grew a lot in 2026), so it hires for everything. Also, the 12 months are not over until January 2027. I will check again.

But look at Amodei’s own quote again. His engineers still work at Anthropic. They just don’t type the code anymore, they direct the model and edit what it writes. The job changed. It didn’t disappear. And the company that knows these models better than anyone is looking for more software engineers than ever.
